title: Pansotti con Salsa di Noci
subtitle: Ligurian herb-filled pasta with walnut cream sauce
excerpt: Pansotti con salsa di noci is a Ligurian stuffed pasta: triangular parcels filled with wild herbs and ricotta, dressed with a smooth, rich sauce of ground walnuts, garlic, bread, and cream. Pansotti means pot-bellied in Ligurian dialect. The walnut sauce is ancient and uniquely Ligurian -- it predates the better-known pesto and is deeply savoury.
sourceNotes: Pansotti con salsa di noci is a traditional dish of the Ligurian Riviera, particularly Genoa and the surrounding region. The walnut sauce (salsa di noci) is one of the oldest recorded Ligurian pasta sauces and appears in medieval Genoese cookery manuscripts. Walnut sauce predates pesto in the Ligurian tradition.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncooked pansotti on a floured tray, then bag. Cook from frozen for 4 to 5 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The walnut sauce keeps in the fridge for 2 days, covered with a film of olive oil.

content.text: Pansotti con salsa di noci is one of the most unusual pasta combinations in Italian cooking: a strongly herb-flavoured filling against a cold, creamy walnut sauce that is served at room temperature rather than heated. The contrast between the hot pasta and the cool, rich sauce works well. The filling traditionally uses a mixture of wild herbs called preboggion in Ligurian -- foraged greens that include borage, wild chard, and nettles. Spinach, borage, and parsley together make a good approximation.

items.prepNote: crusts removed, soaked in water and squeezed dry

content.text: Blanch {{walnuts}} walnuts in boiling water for 1 minute to loosen the skins; drain and rub in a clean cloth to remove as much of the brown papery skin as possible. This reduces bitterness.

Blend the walnuts with the soaked and squeezed {{bread-white}} bread, {{garlic}} garlic, {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} of olive oil, {{double-cream}} of cream, and {{parmesan}} of Parmesan to a smooth, thick sauce. Season with {{salt-table}} salt. The sauce should be thick enough to coat a spoon. Thin with a little pasta water when serving.

Put {{ricotta}} of ricotta in a bowl. Add the {{spinach-frozen}} spinach, {{parsley-flat}} of parsley, {{parmesan}} of Parmesan, {{nutmeg}} of nutmeg, and {{salt-table}} of salt. Mix well and set aside.

Make a pasta dough with {{00-flour}} flour and {{eggs}} eggs. Knead for 10 minutes and rest for 30 minutes. Roll to setting 6 on a pasta machine and cut into 7 cm squares. Place a teaspoon of filling in the centre of each square. Fold each square in half diagonally to make a triangle. Press the edges firmly to seal, making sure no air is trapped inside.

Cook the pansotti in well-salted boiling water for 3 to 4 minutes. Thin the walnut sauce with 3 tablespoons of the pasta cooking water and stir. Lift the pansotti from the water and toss gently in the walnut sauce. Serve with more Parmesan and a little extra olive oil.

items.cause: The walnut skins were not removed.
items.fix: Always blanch walnuts and rub off as much of the papery inner skin as you can before blending. Fresh walnuts in autumn are less bitter than older shelled walnuts.

content.text: Pansotti con salsa di noci is the stuffed pasta of the Ligurian hinterland, distinct from the fish and seafood pasta of the coast. The walnut sauce is one of the oldest recorded sauces in Ligurian cooking, predating pesto by centuries -- walnuts were a major crop of the Ligurian hills before olive groves became dominant. The filling in its traditional form uses preboggion, a Ligurian foraged herb mixture that is specific to the season and the terroir. Outside Liguria, the filling is usually approximated with spinach, borage, and parsley. Pansotti are triangular, which distinguishes them from the square or round ravioli of other regions.
